title: Minimum Absolute Difference
description: Find all pairs achieving the minimum absolute difference in an array, using sorting so only adjacent pairs need to be checked.

blocks.text: Given an array of distinct integers arr, find the minimum absolute difference between any two elements, then return every pair [a, b] (with a < b) achieving that minimum difference. Return the pairs sorted in ascending order.

blocks.caption: After sorting, only adjacent elements can achieve the minimum gap.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","arr[] (distinct integers, may include negatives)"],["Output","All pairs achieving the minimum absolute difference, sorted ascending"],["Key insight","In a sorted array, the minimum gap can only occur between adjacent elements"]]}

blocks.text: Any problem about the minimum (or maximum) difference between pairs of numbers is a strong signal to sort first: once sorted, the closest pair of numbers can only be adjacent in the sorted order, since any non-adjacent pair has at least one element between them that is closer to one side or the other.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This "sort first, then only adjacent pairs matter" insight is one of the most common uses of sorting as a preprocessing step for pairwise comparison problems.

Picture runners lined up in order of their finish times. The two runners with the closest finish times must be standing next to each other in this lineup, since any runner standing between two others is closer to at least one of them than they are to each other.

blocks.caption: The closest pair can only be neighbors once everyone is lined up in order.

items: Sort the array first, O(n log n).
Scan adjacent pairs to find the minimum gap.
Scan again, collecting every adjacent pair whose gap equals that minimum; since the array is sorted, these pairs are automatically in ascending order.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Every adjacent gap is exactly 1, the minimum possible, so all three pairs qualify: [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]], matching the expected output exactly.
A direct approach checks every possible pair of elements, computing the absolute difference for each, to find both the minimum and the qualifying pairs. This is correct but quadratic.

Since the closest pair can only ever be adjacent in sorted order, sorting first reduces the search to just the n-1 adjacent gaps, both for finding the minimum and for collecting all qualifying pairs, each scan being a single linear pass.
Check every pair of elements directly to find the minimum absolute difference, then check every pair again to collect all pairs matching that minimum.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2 log n)","Two O(n^2) scans over all pairs, plus a final sort of the result pairs"],["Space","O(n^2)","Result pairs in the worst case, though typically much smaller"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Checking every pair is unnecessary once it is recognized that only adjacent elements in sorted order can ever achieve the minimum gap.

Sort the array once, O(n log n). Scan adjacent pairs to find the minimum gap, O(n). Scan adjacent pairs again to collect every pair matching that minimum, O(n); since the array is already sorted, these pairs come out in ascending order automatically, no extra sort needed.

items: Sort the array, O(n log n).
First pass over adjacent pairs finds the minimum gap.
Second pass over adjacent pairs collects every pair matching that minimum, already in sorted order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, all-pairs check","O(n^2 log n)","O(n^2)"],["Optimized, sort then adjacent scan","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

items: Sorting is a powerful preprocessing step whenever a problem asks about the minimum or maximum difference between pairs.
Once sorted, only adjacent elements need to be compared, reducing an O(n^2) all-pairs check to an O(n) linear scan.
Results derived from a sorted array often come out already in sorted order, avoiding a separate final sort.

blocks.text: Minimum Absolute Difference is solved by sorting the array first, since the closest pair of numbers can only be adjacent once sorted. One scan finds the minimum gap, and a second scan collects every adjacent pair matching it, already in ascending order, for an overall O(n log n) solution.
